excerpt: Give buyers enough time and clear information to understand the home. A thoughtful viewing plan covers access, occupants, the route through the rooms and the questions that follow.
introduction:
A viewing often goes wrong before anyone reaches the front door. The visitor cannot find the entrance, the building has not approved access or the occupant has been given a different appointment time. None of that helps someone assess whether the property fits their life.

A well-run visit feels straightforward because the practical work has already been done. Buyers can look, ask questions and understand the layout without being rushed through a performance. The seller, broker and occupants also know what to expect. That coordination is especially valuable when the property remains someone's home.
takeaways: Confirm access, timing and occupant arrangements before accepting an appointment.
Let the route explain the layout and leave time for practical questions.
Record specific feedback rather than treating every polite compliment as buying interest.

sections.heading: Make the appointment useful before it starts
sections.body:
Give the broker a concise access sheet covering the correct entrance, visitor parking, reception arrangements and any booking requirements for shared facilities. Check the instructions yourself. A map pin at the centre of a large development may still leave someone a long way from the actual entrance.

Ask prospective buyers what they need to understand from the visit. A household with a large dining table may want to measure the dining area; someone working from home may be interested in room separation and everyday noise. These questions help prepare the visit without requiring unnecessary personal information.

Confirm who will attend and leave a sensible gap before the next appointment. Give visitors a contact for delays and explain how to cancel. If an important space cannot be accessed, say so beforehand and arrange another way to inspect it. Surprising the buyer with a locked room makes the visit less productive.

sections.heading: Agree access with the people living there
sections.body:
Occupied viewings need cooperation. Discuss suitable windows, notice arrangements, pets, working hours and whether the occupants would prefer to remain present. Do not assume a seller's marketing plan overrides the lease or gives unrestricted entry. The actual tenancy and applicable local requirements need to be respected.

Dubai's [Law No. 26 of 2007, Article 28](https://dlp.dubai.gov.ae/Legislation%20Reference/2007/Law%20No.%20%2826%29%20of%202007.html) protects a tenant's right to occupy under a fixed-term lease when ownership changes. A sale and a vacant handover are therefore different questions. The [tenanted-property selling guide](/journal/selling-tenanted-property-uae) addresses that distinction and the need for property-specific advice.

Agree rules for opening cupboards, taking photographs and accessing private areas. Put sensitive paperwork and valuables away before the appointment. If circumstances change, reconfirm the visit rather than relying on an old message. A reliable routine is easier for occupants to accommodate than a succession of last-minute demands.

sections.heading: Choose a route that explains how the home works
sections.body:
Begin with a short orientation at the entrance. Point out the relationship between the main living area, kitchen and bedrooms, then let the buyer see those connections in person. A good route follows the layout rather than jumping between whichever rooms look most impressive.

Leave space for the visitor to stand back and look. Explain practical features such as storage, laundry access and where larger furniture could fit, without claiming a particular item will fit unless it has been measured. Show relevant shared spaces when access is permitted, making their relationship to the private home clear.

Keep the home comfortable and the presentation believable. Strong fragrance, loud music or an excessive number of decorative objects can distract from the property. The [staging guide](/journal/home-staging-uae) offers preparation ideas that help buyers understand the space without disguising its condition.

table.caption: A viewing route built around practical questions
table.note: Adapt the route to the property and agreed access. This is not a required order or a fixed appointment duration.

sections.heading: Answer accurately, including when the answer is not ready
sections.body:
Prepare a short factual pack with the documented area, included fittings, occupancy position and information the owner is authorised to share. Keep it consistent with the listing. If a service cost, alteration approval or maintenance question is unresolved, record it as unresolved rather than estimating confidently during the visit.

Distinguish what you have observed from what needs a professional assessment. A room feeling quiet during a short appointment does not establish its sound-insulation performance. A recently painted ceiling does not explain the history of a leak. Buyers should be able to ask follow-up questions and arrange appropriate checks through the agreed process.

Avoid turning every question into a sales response. Someone asking about afternoon sun needs information about the room, not a general statement that the home is bright and luxurious. A clear answer, or a commitment to obtain the right document, helps the buyer make a more informed decision.

sections.heading: Treat an open house as a separate operational choice
sections.body:
Several appointments grouped together may reduce repeated preparation, but an open house also needs a plan for reception, access, privacy and the number of people inside. Consider whether the occupants and building can accommodate it. More visitors at once can make detailed questions harder to handle.

[DLD's real-estate advertisement permit service](https://backoffice.dubailand.gov.ae/en/eservices/real-estate-ad-permit/) includes open-house events among its listed permit types. For a Dubai property, have the responsible broker confirm the applicable permission and arrangements before promoting an event. Do not treat an ordinary viewing appointment and a publicly advertised event as automatically interchangeable.

Agree who supervises each area and how attendees are recorded with appropriate privacy care. Keep keys and documents controlled. If the home is small or access is restricted, individual appointments may provide a clearer experience. Choose the format for the property and people involved, not simply because an event sounds more ambitious.

sections.heading: Turn the follow-up into useful information
sections.body:
After the visit, ask what the buyer understood well and what remains unclear. Record specific objections in their own context: a bedroom may be too small for that household, or a move-in date may not match their plans. Those are different issues from an inaccurate floor plan or unanswered maintenance question.

Look for patterns across several visits without overreacting to one preference. If buyers repeatedly cannot understand the dining layout, improve the photographs or plan. If the same cost question keeps arising, obtain the relevant evidence. A useful feedback record separates presentation problems from features the seller cannot change.

Finally, close the loop on promised answers. Send the requested information through the broker and keep a record of what was provided. Do not pressure someone to make an offer before an important question is resolved. A well-organised viewing ends with a clear next step, whether that is a second visit, further checks or an honest decision that the home is unsuitable.
